item.research_question: What are the high-temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy superalloy (HESA) with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, and how do they compare to conventional Ni-based superalloys?
item.processing_route: Vacuum-arc-melting followed by directional-solidification; Solution-heat-treatment at 1210 °C for 10 h; Primary aging at 1000 °C for 3 h; Secondary aging at 800 °C for 20 h
item.test_conditions: Tensile tests at strain rate 10^-3 sec^-1 from room temperature to 950 °C; Creep tests at 750, 850, and 982 °C under constant stress of 159 MPa
key_findings: Tensile yield strength of HESA surpasses reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures, reaching 840 MPa at room temperature.
Creep rupture life of HESA at 982 °C is approximately 114 hours, comparable to first-generation Ni-based superalloys like Rene' 80 (118 h).
The γ' precipitate volume fraction is 69 vol% with an average size of 290 nm in the heat-treated condition.
Lattice misfit (δ) between γ and γ' at 982 °C is calculated to be 0.08% (positive misfit).
The creep activation energy (Q) for HESA is estimated at 290 kJ/mol, higher than CMSX-2 (230 kJ/mol).
At 982 °C, the creep curves are dominated by tertiary creep behavior with no obvious primary creep regime.
Stacking fault energy (SFE) of the HESA matrix is estimated around 0.7 J/m^2, lower than CMSX-2 (0.9 J/m^2).
Anti-phase boundary (APB) energy of the γ' phase in HESA is 0.22 J/m^2, higher than CMSX-2 (0.19 J/m^2).
item.mechanism: HESA is strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. At 982 °C, positive misfit yields parallel raft microstructure, leading to tertiary creep dominance. At lower temperatures, deformation occurs via thermally activated bypassing of dislocations around un-rafted γ' precipitates, facilitated by sluggish diffusion in the high entropy matrix.
item.limitations: The as heat-treated γ' size (290 nm) is smaller than the optimized size (approx. 390 nm), limiting peak strength; the positive lattice misfit leads to parallel rafting which may increase creep rates compared to negative misfit alloys at high temperatures.
item.future_work: Study the non-isothermal creep behavior of HESA; minor addition of γ partitioning elements like Mo and Re to achieve negative lattice misfit for N-type rafting and solid-solution strengthening.
quotes: The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures
Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C
The creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior
